/-!
# Beurling primes

*References:*
 - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling_zeta_function)
 - [Beurling Zeta Functions, Generalised Primes, and Fractal Membranes](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0410270)
-/

open Filter

/-- A sequence of real numbers `1 < a 0 < a 1 < ...` is called a set of Beurling prime numbers if
it tends to infinity. -/
noncomputable def IsBeurlingPrimes (a : ℕ → ℝ) : Prop :=
  1 < a 0 ∧ StrictMono a ∧ Tendsto a atTop atTop

/-- A Beurling integer is a number of the form `∏ i, (a i) ^ (k i)` for a given sequence `a` and a
finitely-supported sequence of naturals `k`. -/
def beurlingInteger (a : ℕ → ℝ) (k : ℕ →₀ ℕ) : ℝ := k.prod fun x y ↦ (a x) ^ y

@[simp] theorem beurlingInteger_def (a k) : beurlingInteger a k =  k.prod fun x y ↦ (a x) ^ y := rfl

/-- The set of Beurling integers are numbers of the form `∏ i, (a i) ^ (k i)`, where `k` has
finite support. -/
def BeurlingIntegers (a : ℕ → ℝ) : Set ℝ := .range (beurlingInteger a)

theorem beurlingInteger_mem (a k) : beurlingInteger a k ∈ BeurlingIntegers a := by
  simpa using ⟨k, rfl⟩

/-- Every element of the sequence `a` is a Beurling integer. -/
lemma generator_mem_beurling (a : ℕ → ℝ) (i : ℕ) : a i ∈ BeurlingIntegers a :=
  ⟨Finsupp.single i 1, by aesop⟩

/-- The set of Beurling integers is closed under multiplication. -/
lemma mul_mem_beurling {a : ℕ → ℝ} {x y : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ BeurlingIntegers a)
    (hy : y ∈ BeurlingIntegers a) : x * y ∈ BeurlingIntegers a := by
  obtain ⟨k, rfl⟩ := hx
  obtain ⟨l, rfl⟩ := hy
  exact ⟨k + l, by simp [Finsupp.prod_add_index', pow_add]⟩

/-- The set of Beurling integers is closed under taking powers. -/
lemma pow_mem_beurling {a : ℕ → ℝ} {x : ℝ} (k : ℕ) (hx : x ∈ BeurlingIntegers a) :
    x ^ k ∈ BeurlingIntegers a := by
  induction k with
  | zero => exact ⟨0, by norm_num⟩
  | succ k ih => simpa [pow_succ'] using mul_mem_beurling hx ih

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/951.lean:67–70, `(BeurlingIntegers a ∩ .Iic x).ncard` counts distinct real values, not generalized integers with multiplicity. `StrictMono a` does not make `beurlingInteger a` injective. For example, let `a n = (n : ℝ) + 2`. This satisfies `IsBeurlingPrimes`, but 4 has the distinct factorizations `single 0 2` and `single 2 1`. Its set `BeurlingIntegers a` is exactly the positive ordinary integers, so the displayed counting hypothesis holds with count `⌊x⌋₊`, while the conclusion fails at index 2 (4 ≠ 5). The entire Lean statement is refuted without `sorry` in `/workspace/review/scratch.lean`, theorem `BeurlingReview.beurling_variant_false`. This is a counting-definition error, not a status issue.
findings.source_evidence: Hilberdink–Lapidus, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0410270, §1.1, equation (1.2), defines the generalized-integer counting function and explicitly says that the sums count multiplicities: “Similarly for [the sum over generalized integers].” https://www.erdosproblems.com/951 states Beurling’s conjecture that the generalized-integer count `x + o(log x)` forces the ordinary primes; see also Erdős, A survey of problems in combinatorial number theory, p.103, equation (12), https://users.renyi.hu/~p_erdos/1980-03.pdf.
findings.suggested_fix: Count exponent vectors rather than their image: replace the counting expression by `({k : ℕ →₀ ℕ | beurlingInteger a k ≤ x}.ncard : ℝ)`. This preserves multiplicities, including different factorizations with the same value. Keep `BeurlingIntegers` as the underlying set for membership and closure lemmas. The required finiteness of the exponent-vector sublevel sets under `IsBeurlingPrimes a` is proved in the scratch file.

findings.description: Lines 34–37 deliberately define only repetition-free systems by requiring `StrictMono a`. The general Beurling-prime notion in the cited literature permits repeated primes. For example, `a n = max ((n : ℝ) + 1) 2`, namely 2,2,3,4,…, has first term greater than 1, is nondecreasing, and tends to infinity, but fails this predicate. These facts are proved in `BeurlingReview.standard_but_not_strict`. Removing repeated terms is not an equivalent reindexing: it changes multiplicities and the associated Euler product. Because strict increase is explicitly documented and is appropriate for the main Erdős 951 use, this is flagged as a documented restriction of the reusable notion rather than a docstring/Lean mismatch.
findings.source_evidence: Hilberdink–Lapidus, https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0410270, abstract and §1.1: a generalized prime system satisfies `1 < p₁ ≤ p₂ ≤ ⋯` and tends to infinity. Its §2 “Conditional Examples” explicitly includes Gaussian-integer prime systems in which rational primes congruent to 1 modulo 4 occur with multiplicity two. The cited Wikipedia article, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling_zeta_function, likewise allows any sequence of reals greater than 1 tending to infinity.
findings.suggested_fix: For the standard general notion, use `1 < a 0 ∧ Monotone a ∧ Tendsto a atTop atTop`. If repetition-free systems are intentionally distinguished, retain that restricted predicate separately and provide the general predicate allowing repetitions.

findings.description: In FormalConjectures/ErdosProblems/951.lean:39–44, the docstring says that `Erdos951Prop a` and `1 < a 0` suffice, but the theorem additionally assumes `hm : StrictMono a`. That assumption is not implied by the two documented hypotheses: permuting the first two ordinary primes preserves the separation property and `1 < a 0`, but destroys strict monotonicity. The proved Lean statement is correct; its docstring omits a necessary hypothesis.
findings.source_evidence: The local docstring says “If `a` has property `Erdos951Prop` and `1 < a 0`, then `a` is a set of Beurling prime numbers.” The declaration immediately below also requires `StrictMono a`. The cited problem https://www.erdosproblems.com/951 explicitly starts with the increasing sequence `1 < a₁ < ⋯`.
findings.suggested_fix: Change the docstring to say that `a` is strictly increasing, has `Erdos951Prop`, and satisfies `1 < a 0`.

reformulations.difference: Membership is encoded using the range of products over finitely-supported exponent vectors, rather than the finite-prefix products written in the paper.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: For a finitely-supported vector, choose a prefix containing its support; every added factor has exponent zero and equals 1. Conversely, extend the exponents of any finite-prefix product by zero to obtain a finitely-supported vector. The all-zero vector produces 1, which the source also permits through its nonnegative exponents. `BeurlingReview.mem_iff_finite_prefix` proves this membership equivalence; `mem_iff_submonoid_closure` also identifies the set with Mathlib’s generated multiplicative submonoid. This equivalence concerns the set of values, not multiplicity-aware counting.

reformulations.difference: The cutoff uses `BeurlingIntegers a ∩ Set.Iic x`, whereas the source describes the interval `[1,x]`.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Under `IsBeurlingPrimes a`, every generator is greater than 1. Every product with natural exponents is therefore at least 1, including the empty product, which equals 1. Consequently intersection with `Iic x` is exactly intersection with `Icc 1 x`. This set equality is proved in `BeurlingReview.interval_agreement`; the omitted lower endpoint is not an additional defect.

review.notes: Checked all three definitions and five proved lemmas, all declaration-name use sites, and Mathlib for an existing Beurling notion. The only substantive problem-file use is Erdős 951. The set-valued `BeurlingIntegers` correctly implements its documented membership/closure meaning; the definite error occurs when its cardinality is used as the standard counting function. The final `/workspace/review/scratch.lean` compiles successfully and proves the counterexample, the reformulations, and finiteness of both exponent-vector and value sublevel sets without `sorryAx`. Thus no infinite-set `ncard` default is reachable under the predicate. The source still records the main Erdős question as open and explicitly discusses the eventual-in-x version chosen by Lean. It does not give an explicit current resolution of the separate Beurling conjecture, so no stale-status claim is made for that variant. The reviewed file and its problem use were not modified.

The existing set of product values cannot preserve multiplicities through its cardinality.

submission.summary: Added `beurlingIntegerCounting`, which counts exponent vectors separately, and proved `IsBeurlingPrimes.finite_beurlingInteger_le` to justify finiteness. Existing definitions and lemmas were left unchanged. A scratch test verifies that the new count detects the repeated factorization of 4; the required compilation command reports no errors or warnings.

@[expose] public section

/-!
# Beurling primes

*References:*
 - [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beurling_zeta_function)

lemma mul_mem_beurling {a : ℕ → ℝ} {x y : ℝ} (hx : x ∈ BeurlingIntegers a)
    (hy : y ∈ BeurlingIntegers a) : x * y ∈ BeurlingIntegers a := by
  obtain ⟨k, rfl⟩ := hx

  exact ⟨k + l, by simp [Finsupp.prod_add_index', pow_add]⟩

    x ^ k ∈ BeurlingIntegers a := by
  induction k with
  | zero => exact ⟨0, by norm_num⟩
  | succ k ih => simpa [pow_succ'] using mul_mem_beurling hx ih

/-- The number of Beurling integers at most `x`, counted with multiplicity. Distinct
finitely-supported exponent vectors are counted separately, even when their products agree.
The zero vector contributes the integer `1` when `1 ≤ x`.

For `IsBeurlingPrimes a`, the set being counted is finite. As with `Set.ncard`, the value is
`0` if this set is infinite. -/
noncomputable def beurlingIntegerCounting (a : ℕ → ℝ) (x : ℝ) : ℕ :=
  {k : ℕ →₀ ℕ | beurlingInteger a k ≤ x}.ncard

/-- A Beurling prime sequence has only finitely many exponent vectors whose products are
at most a given real number, so its multiplicity-aware counting function is finite. -/
theorem IsBeurlingPrimes.finite_beurlingInteger_le {a : ℕ → ℝ} (ha : IsBeurlingPrimes a)
    (x : ℝ) : {k : ℕ →₀ ℕ | beurlingInteger a k ≤ x}.Finite := by
  classical
  have ha₁ (i : ℕ) : 1 ≤ a i := ha.1.le.trans (ha.2.1.monotone (Nat.zero_le i))
  obtain ⟨N, hN⟩ := tendsto_atTop_atTop.mp ha.2.2 (x + 1)
  obtain ⟨M, hM⟩ := tendsto_atTop_atTop.mp
    (tendsto_pow_atTop_atTop_of_one_lt ha.1) (x + 1)
  let bound : ℕ →₀ ℕ := Finsupp.onFinset (Finset.range N)
    (fun i => if i < N then M else 0) (by simp +contextual)
  apply (Set.finite_Icc (0 : ℕ →₀ ℕ) bound).subset
  intro k hk
  refine ⟨bot_le, (Finsupp.le_iff k bound).mpr fun i hi => ?_⟩
  have hpow : a i ^ k i ≤ x := by
    have h := Finset.prod_le_prod_of_subset_of_one_le
      (f := fun j => a j ^ k j) (s := {i}) (t := k.support)
      (by simpa using hi)
      (fun j _ => pow_nonneg (zero_le_one.trans (ha₁ j)) _)
      (fun j _ _ => one_le_pow₀ (ha₁ j))
    refine le_trans ?_ hk
    simpa [beurlingInteger, Finsupp.prod] using h
  have hai : a i ≤ x :=
    (le_self_pow₀ (ha₁ i) (Finsupp.mem_support_iff.mp hi)).trans hpow
  have hin : i < N := lt_of_not_ge fun h =>
    (not_lt_of_ge hai) ((lt_add_one x).trans_le (hN i h))
  have hp0 : a 0 ^ k i ≤ x :=
    (pow_le_pow_left₀ (zero_lt_one.trans ha.1).le
      (ha.2.1.monotone (Nat.zero_le i)) _).trans hpow
  have hkim : k i < M := lt_of_not_ge fun h =>
    (not_lt_of_ge hp0) ((lt_add_one x).trans_le (hM (k i) h))
  simpa [bound, hin] using hkim.le
